common_name: Georgia Scarlet Bat-Face Cuphea (All-Red Batface Cigar Flower)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants once soil has warmed after the last frost; this selection tolerates heat well but establishes fastest when nights stay reliably above 55°F.

directions: Georgia Scarlet was bred at the University of Georgia to concentrate red pigment across the whole flower, replacing the two pale 'ears' of the wild bat-face form with solid crimson-purple coloring while keeping the same one-sided racemes and continuous bloom habit. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil and pinch young plants once to encourage a denser, more floriferous mound. It rebounds quickly from light frost damage in zone 9 and can be cut back hard in late winter to renew growth. Excellent in mixed containers and hanging baskets where its trailing-mounded habit and hummingbird traffic can be viewed up close.

planting.note: Set out transplants after soil has warmed following the last frost; this compact selection fills in quickly and is well suited to edging beds or mass planting.

directions: Allyson is a naturally dense, uniform selection of Mexican heather bred for landscape bedding use, holding its lavender-pink, tubular flowers over glossy, needle-like foliage from early summer straight through to first frost without deadheading. Its foliage stays full to the ground, so it needs no facer plants to hide bare lower stems the way older seed-grown forms sometimes do. It tolerates both consistent moisture and short dry spells once rooted in, and while it is usually grown as a warm-season annual outside the Gulf Coast, established clumps often resprout from the crown after a mild zone 9 winter. Shear lightly in early spring to refresh growth before the summer flush begins.

planting.note: Plant after all danger of frost has passed; this wider-spreading white form works well as a low, informal border edge or groundcover in warm-season beds.

directions: This white-flowered sport of Mexican heather carries the same fine, fern-textured foliage and reddish-brown stems as the species but swaps the typical lilac-purple flowers for masses of tiny star-shaped white blooms that open continuously from late spring through late summer. Its habit spreads noticeably wider than it grows tall, making it useful as a low informal edging or filler between larger perennials rather than a strictly upright bedding plant. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom; light afternoon shade is tolerated in the hottest inland gardens. Cut back hard after a freeze in zone 9, since it typically regrows readily from the base in spring.

planting.note: Plant after the last frost once nights are consistently mild; this species tolerates light afternoon shade better than most Cuphea and appreciates a break from the most intense midday sun.

directions: Cuphea cyanea produces tubular, inch-long flowers in a striking three-color combination of hot pink, yellow, and near-black purple that gives the small upper petals a whimsical 'ears' appearance, distinct from both the orange cigar-tip pattern of C. ignea and the bat-face shape of C. llavea. It grows into a rounder, somewhat larger shrub than most garden cuphea and benefits from a light pinch when young to encourage branching. Give it even moisture through the growing season for the heaviest bloom, though established plants handle brief dry spells without serious setback. It is reliably hardy to about zone 9b and can be overwintered as a potted specimen or brought indoors as a houseplant farther north.
